[page/5/Text/7] Participants from Eastern and Western Canada were recruited through newspaper advertisements and brochures mailed to community service agencies for involvement in this study.

evidence.section_title: Being in the Safety Zone: Emotional Experiences of Suicidal Adolescents and Emerging Adults
evidence.quote: This study examined how previously suicidal adolescents and emerging adults perceived their emotional experiences while being suicidal. Forty-one females and 9 males previously suicidal between the ages of 15 and 24 were interviewed. Qualitative data were analyzed using a grounded theory approach. Three major themes were identified in participants' perceptions of their emotional experiences: (a) overwhelming despair, (b) shame and self-loathing, and (c) alienation and personal isolation. These emotional states were viewed within the multidimensional process of responding to emotions. Participants' inability to deal with intense negative emotions appeared to be related to their suicidal state. Keywords: attempted suicide; suicidal ideation; adolescents; emotional experience; emotion regulation

[page/5/Text/7] Selection criteria for participants included (a) being suicidal between the ages of 15 and 24; (b) having been suicidal within the past 3 years; (c) being free of suicidal thoughts and feelings for a minimum of 6 months prior to being interviewed; and (d) willingness to participate in research. [page/5/Text/8] Fifty participants, 41 females and 9 males, were included in the study. At the time of the interview, participants were between 15 and 27 years of age with a mean age of 21. evidence.section_title: Being in the Safety Zone: Emotional Experiences of Suicidal Adolescents and Emerging Adults
evidence.quote: Three major themes were identified in participants' perceptions of their emotional experiences: (a) overwhelming despair, (b) shame and self-loathing, and (c) alienation and personal isolation. These emotional states were viewed within the multidimensional process of responding to emotions. Participants' inability to deal with intense negative emotions appeared to be related to their suicidal state.

[page/6/Text/4] Open-ended questions then focused on the individual's thoughts, feelings, and behaviors while becoming and overcoming suicidality. Examples include "Tell me about the feelings you had while you were suicidal"; "How did you express your emotions when distressed?"; "What did you do to cope with your emotions?"; and "How would you describe yourself as a suicidal person?"

[/page/14/Text/4] Given that difficult relationships at home were identified as contributing to distressing emotional experiences, it is not surprising that a positive change of environment frequently involved moving away from the family home. [/page/14/Text/4] For the participants in this study, the process of overcoming suicidality and liberating themselves from predominantly negative emotional states occurred within the contexts of a change in environment, the development of at least one stable and supportive relationship, and an increased understanding of personal control.

[/page/15/Text/6] This study suggests that participants' experiences of difficult emotions and their responses to intense negative emotions involved a complex and dynamic process of interactions that shaped negative self-perceptions and maladaptive coping strategies. Disturbing emotions were reported to dominate the lives of these individuals during the time they were suicidal, and participants' perceptions of becoming suicidal centered around three main themes of emotional experience: overwhelming despair, shame and selfloathing, and alienation. [/page/16/Text/2] emotions characteristic of the theme of overwhelming despair. In addition, it was reported that a growing sense of control over both negative emotional states and negative interpersonal interactions was obtained through the support provided by trusting relationships. [/page/16/Text/3] It is interesting that shame was spontaneously discussed by our participants and was identified as contributing to the reinforcement of negative self-perceptions, self-loathing, lack of personal value, and anxiety. The experience of shame compelled participants to keep their negative emotions secret and served to restrain them from help-seeking behavior. [/page/16/Text/4] Consistent with this research, participants in this study reported suicidal ideation to act as a barrier to help-seeking behavior. It is important to note that participants attributed difficulties with help seeking to experiences of shame, worthlessness, and anxiety. Shame reactions acted to restrain suicidal individuals from both seeking help and expressing their needs, making them hypersensitive to negative attitudes of others and motivating an urge to flee and avoid being with other people (Wiklander et al., 2003). Consistent with Arnett (2004), who discusses the effect of leaving a distressing family situation, for the participants in this study, removal from the distressing environment, whether it was home, school, or community, often reduced the sense of vulnerability and allowed participants to recognize and use external resources that facilitated their healing. [/page/17/Text/2] consistent with reports in this study whereby emotions were experienced as overwhelming during the adolescent years and difficulty with regulating emotions appropriately was related. Little prior experience with intense negative emotions contributed to difficulties in expressing and dealing with emotions. However, once a trusting relationship was developed, openly discussing negative emotions provided participants with an expanded understanding of their experiences. [/page/17/Text/3] Many of those interviewed in this study described having families in which emotions were not expressed and personal feelings were ignored or kept hidden. They perceived their parents as failing to model emotional control and expression and neglecting to teach the value of emotional communication. These participants had difficulty describing their emotions while they were suicidal and lacked the vocabulary to describe emotional states. Their struggle to discriminate and differentiate between emotions contributed to feelings of helplessness that were not necessarily resolved within the family but were ameliorated when another significant relationship was established (Bostik & Everall, in press). [/page/17/Text/4] Affect dysregulation has been associated with suicidal behavior during adolescence, suggesting that youth who attempt suicide may have a diminished capacity to manage their internal states and may use suicide attempts as a means of reducing intolerable emotional states (Zlotnick et al., 1997). Reports of the experiences of participants in this study support this contention, as most perceived their intense, distressing emotions to dominate every aspect of their lives and saw no available relief other than suicide. When experiencing overwhelmingly negative emotions, participants tended to interpret difficulties with emotional regulation [/page/18/Text/2] and expression as signifying personal inadequacy. Increasingly, participants in this study focused on suicide as the only option that would save them from their intense negative emotional reality.
